407.title: Acharei Mot: the goat to Azazel (Leviticus 16:21–22)
407.hook: wrongs are confessed over a goat sent into the wilderness
407.howItsDone: The goat ritual ended with the Temple; on Yom Kippur the Avodah service retells it, and on Rosh Hashanah many Jews practice tashlich, saying verses beside flowing water, and some cast crumbs into it, as a picture of sending wrongs away.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Acharei Mot, even the high priest could not enter at all times. Your line was not at all times. Today, the strangest moment of the holiest day.

Scapegoat. In English it's the one who takes the blame for everybody: the intern blamed for the server crash, the kid blamed for the broken lamp. It's become a word for unfairness. But it started as something else entirely, in Leviticus 16. On Yom Kippur, two goats stand before the high priest, as alike as possible, the rabbis said, in look, in size, in price. Lots are drawn. One is marked for God. And the other is marked with a word nobody has ever fully explained.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TAKES THE BLAME.` → `TWO GOATS, AS ALIKE AS POSSIBLE.` → `ONE FOR GOD, ONE FOR AZAZEL.`

segments.voice: The high priest lays both hands on the head of the living goat and confesses over it all the wrongs of the people. Then a man appointed for the job leads it into the wilderness, carrying those wrongs, the text says, to a land cut off. The lot says: for Azazel. What is Azazel? Honestly, nobody knows for certain. The Talmud reads it as the name of a place, the hardest, steepest of mountains, a cliff, and Rashi follows that. Others, ancient and modern, read it as the name of a wilderness being. Commentators have argued about it ever since, and the text doesn't settle it. And scapegoat? When William Tyndale put the Torah into English in 1530, he read the Hebrew as ez ozel, the goat that goes away, and wrote scapegoat: the goat that escapes. So the English word comes from one translator's reading of a puzzle. The Mishnah describes a crimson thread tied to the goat, and records a tradition that when the goat reached the wilderness, a crimson thread tied at the sanctuary turned white, and the people took it as a sign of forgiveness. Notice what the ritual is not. Nobody blames the goat. It isn't punished for being bad. It's a vehicle: the wrongs are named out loud, then carried far away.
screen: `BOTH HANDS ON ITS HEAD.` · `AZAZEL: A CLIFF, OR A NAME?` · `TYNDALE'S SCAPEGOAT.` · `THE THREAD TURNED WHITE.` · then, large: `SEND IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've done that you're still carrying: not your whole life, one thing. Write it on a scrap of paper in a few plain words, the way the high priest named the wrongs out loud, read it once, then tear it up small and throw it away. Tomorrow comes what tearing it up can't do; for today, let it go into the wilderness.
Azazel. The mysterious destination of the second goat on Yom Kippur, carrying the people's wrongs into the wilderness. A cliff, or a name: the sources differ.
Your line: send it away. The wrongs are named out loud, then carried off. See you tomorrow.

408.title: Acharei Mot: ask the person first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
408.hook: Yom Kippur atones between people and God, but wrongs between people need their forgiveness
408.howItsDone: In the days before Yom Kippur, many Jews ask family, friends and coworkers for forgiveness directly, and some recite a prayer of forgiving others, Tefillah Zakkah, before Kol Nidre.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Azazel: the goat that carried the wrongs away. Your line was send it away. Today, the catch I promised.

A sharp word at dinner. A man snaps at his brother, says something cruel. Later, alone, he sits quietly, sincerely sorry, and asks God to forgive him. He feels lighter. Done. But his brother is still in the next room, still stung, and nobody has said a word to him. Leviticus 16 promises that on Yom Kippur, the people will be cleansed of all their sins. All of them. The rabbis read that promise very closely, and found a condition hidden in two words.
screen: `SORRY, BUT ONLY TO GOD.` → `HIS BROTHER, STILL STUNG.` → `A CONDITION IN TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Leviticus 16:30 says that on this day atonement will be made for you, from all your sins, before the Lord. In the Mishnah, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah leans on those two words: before the Lord. Wrongs between a person and God, he teaches, Yom Kippur atones for. But wrongs between a person and another person, Yom Kippur does not atone for, until you make it right with them. Not even Yom Kippur skips that step. Maimonides spells out the steps. Repay what you owe. Go to the person and ask their forgiveness. If they refuse, come back with three friends and try again, up to three times. If they still refuse, you've done your part, and the burden passes to them. And he adds a word to the one being asked: don't be cruel. When someone sincerely asks, forgive, even if it's hard. Because of this teaching, the days before Yom Kippur can fill with phone calls, emails, awkward conversations at the kiddush table. People ask each other, plainly: if I've hurt you this year, I'm sorry, please forgive me. Yesterday's practice tore up a wrong and sent it away. In the Mishnah's terms, that kind of turning belongs to what lies between a person and God. But if the wrong had a person on the other end, the order is clear. Ask the person first.

409.title: Acharei Mot: live by them (Leviticus 18:5)
409.hook: "which if a man do, he shall live by them"; so saving a life overrides almost every law (Yoma 85b)
409.howItsDone: Jewish law requires setting aside Shabbat, fasts and most other commandments to save a life or treat serious illness; observant doctors, nurses and volunteer ambulance crews work on Shabbat for this reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Acharei Mot, the Mishnah's condition: wrongs between people need their forgiveness. Your line was ask the person first. Today, the end of the portion, and a rule about the rules.

It's Saturday morning in an observant neighborhood. A man who wouldn't turn on a light switch on Shabbat, who walks to synagogue in the rain rather than drive, sees his neighbor collapse on the sidewalk. He pulls out his phone, calls an ambulance, and does everything the dispatcher tells him. Nobody who knows Jewish law would blink; they'd say he did exactly what the law requires. The reason goes back to a few words in Leviticus 18, and to a rabbi who read them very carefully.
screen: `A MAN COLLAPSES ON SHABBAT.` → `THE PHONE COMES OUT.` → `EXACTLY WHAT THE LAW REQUIRES.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God's statutes and ordinances are the ones "which if a man do, he shall live by them." In the Talmud, the sages ask where we learn that saving a life overrides Shabbat. Several answers are offered, and the one left standing is Samuel's: he shall live by them, and not die by them. The commandments are for living. If keeping one would cost a life, the life comes first. Jewish law calls this pikuach nefesh. Nefesh is a life, a soul. Pikuach comes from a picture in the Mishnah: rubble falls on someone on Shabbat, and you don't know whether they're under it, or alive. You clear the rubble anyway. That clearing, uncovering, is pikuach. Even a doubt about danger to life is enough. There are limits. The Talmud names three things a person may not do even to save their own life: worship idols, commit murder, or commit certain forbidden sexual acts. Almost everything else gives way. Fasting on Yom Kippur, Shabbat, the food laws: a sick person may be required to set them aside. And the idea reaches into ordinary days. Maimonides counts keeping your body healthy as part of serving God, because you can't do much of anything if you're broken. Live by them, not in spite of them.

segments.voice: Notice your body: where is it tired, tight, ignored? Not as self-improvement; as taking care of a life.
Pikuach nefesh. Saving a life: the principle, drawn from live by them, that protecting life overrides almost every other commandment.

410.title: Kedoshim: holiness for everyone (Leviticus 19:2)
410.hook: holiness is spoken to the whole congregation, not only to priests
410.howItsDone: Kedoshim is read in synagogue in the spring, often together with Acharei Mot, and Leviticus 19 is often taught in Jewish ethics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pikuach nefesh: the law is for living. Your line was live by them. Today, a new portion, and a chapter spoken to everyone.

For long stretches of Leviticus, holiness has had a dress code: linen garments, a golden plate, a turban. It's had an address: the sanctuary, the altar, the room behind the curtain. And much of the time it's had a small cast: Aaron and his sons. The call to be holy was heard once already, back in chapter eleven, about food. Still, a shepherd or a weaver listening might wonder whether holiness was mostly the priests' business. Then chapter nineteen opens, and it is spoken to everyone.
screen: `HOLINESS HAD A DRESS CODE.` → `MOSTLY A PRIESTLY CAST.` → `CHAPTER NINETEEN SPEAKS TO ALL.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Speak unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, and say unto them: Ye shall be holy; for I the LORD your God am holy." All the congregation. Not the priests. Everyone. The portion takes its name from that call: Kedoshim, holy ones. Rashi, drawing on an older midrash, says this chapter was taught with the whole people gathered together, because most of the essentials of the Torah depend on it. And read on: the chapter doesn't send anyone to the altar. Revere your mother and your father. Keep the Sabbath. Don't steal, don't lie to each other. Pay a hired worker the same day; don't keep his wages overnight. Rise before the gray head and honor the old. Keep honest scales and honest weights. Holiness, in Kedoshim, sits in a paycheck, a grocery scale, a seat given up on the bus. The chapter switches back and forth between what we'd call ritual and what we'd call ethics, sometimes verse to verse, and never marks the difference. Some teachers read that as the point: the holy and the decent aren't two departments. Over the next days, I'll take a few of these verses one at a time. For today, just the opening: the call is to everyone, and it lands in ordinary places.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION.` · `TAUGHT TO THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY.` · `WAGES, SCALES, THE GRAY HEAD.` · `RITUAL AND ETHICS, UNMARKED.` · then, large: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.`

segments.voice: Pick something completely ordinary from your day: paying someone, answering an email, giving change at the register, cooking dinner. Kedoshim. Holy ones: the portion that calls the whole people to holiness, and finds it in wages, scales and honoring the old.
Your line: holiness for everyone. No dress code, no altar required. Day four hundred ten.

411.title: Kedoshim: the corners of the field (Leviticus 19:9–10)
411.hook: leave the field's edges and fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger
411.howItsDone: Farmers in Israel who keep the agricultural laws still leave pe'ah, and some Jews outside farming see tzedakah, giving to those in need, as continuing the same commandment; the Mishnah's tractate Peah, which opens with the list of things without measure, is recited in the morning prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kedoshim opened with a call to everyone. Your line was holiness for everyone. Today, the first of those ordinary places: a field at harvest.

A field of barley at harvest, gold to the edges. The owner planted it, waited on the rain, and counts every stalk as his. The harvesters are swinging their sickles toward the far end. In the Book of Ruth, a young widow from Moab, poor and far from home, walks into a field like this one, behind the harvesters, and starts picking up what they drop. Nobody chases her off. Because the owner of the field had been told, long before, to leave her something.
screen: `GOLD TO THE EDGES.` → `A WIDOW BEHIND THE HARVESTERS.` → `NOBODY CHASES HER OFF.`

segments.voice: Leviticus 19 says: when you reap, don't reap the corner of your field all the way. That corner is called pe'ah, the edge. Don't go back for the gleanings, the stalks that drop as you cut. In the vineyard, don't strip every last cluster, and don't pick up the fallen grapes. The reason, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God." How big a corner? The Torah doesn't say. The Mishnah opens its tractate on the subject with a list of things that have no fixed measure, and pe'ah is first on the list, next to acts of kindness and Torah study. Then the rabbis set a floor: at least one sixtieth of the field. And a detail about dignity: the owner doesn't hand the corner out to people he likes. It's left standing, and those in need come and harvest it themselves, waiting on nobody's favor. Then the story it made possible. Ruth, gleaning, ends up in the field of Boaz, a relative of her mother-in-law Naomi's late husband. He tells his workers to let some stalks fall on purpose for her. Their marriage, the Book of Ruth says, leads to King David. A line of kings, traced back to a field where the poor were allowed to gather.

segments.voice: Think about the fields of your own life: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your space. Let one corner come to mind.
Pe'ah. The corner of the field left unharvested, so the poor and the stranger can come and gather for themselves.
Your line: leave the corners. What's left standing is theirs to gather. See you tomorrow.

412.title: Kedoshim: no stumbling block (Leviticus 19:14)
412.hook: don't put a stumbling block before the blind; the rabbis read it as never misleading anyone
412.howItsDone: Jewish law applies lifnei iver, the stumbling-block principle, to advice, business dealings and helping others do wrong, and it appears in rabbinic rulings on everything from selling dangerous goods to giving biased counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, pe'ah, the corners of the field. Your line was leave the corners. Today, a verse that starts literal and keeps growing.

A friend is about to buy a used car, and asks what you think. You happen to know the transmission is shot. You also happen to want that car yourself, and if they pass, the price will drop. So you say, eh, I'd look at other options. Nobody would ever know why you said it. Nothing you said was even false. Leviticus 19 has a short verse about a blind man and an obstacle in the road. The rabbis read it, and found your friend and the car inside it.
screen: `A FRIEND ASKS ABOUT A CAR.` → `NOBODY WOULD EVER KNOW.` → `A BLIND MAN AND A ROAD.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling-block before the blind, but thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD." Plainly, it means what it says. Don't trip someone who can't see it coming. Don't curse someone who can't hear it. Then the widening. The Sifra, an early rabbinic commentary on Leviticus, reads the blind as anyone blind in a matter, anyone who can't see what you can see. If someone asks your advice, don't give advice that isn't good for them. Its example: don't say sell your field and buy a donkey, when you're secretly planning to buy that field yourself. The Talmud stretches it further: don't hand a cup of wine to someone who has vowed not to drink. Don't help another person do the wrong they're already reaching for. A stumbling block can be an offer, a nudge, a door held open. And why does the verse close with fear thy God? Rashi answers: because nobody else can check. Only you know whether your advice was honest or self-serving. That's exactly what makes the other person blind in this matter, and why the verse hands the case to God. Today the principle is cited in Jewish discussions of business ethics, financial advice and selling to people who can't judge what they're buying.
screen: `DON'T TRIP THE ONE WHO CAN'T SEE.` · `BLIND IN A MATTER.` · `NO CUP FOR THE ONE WHO VOWED.` · `ONLY YOU KNOW YOUR INTENT.` · then, large: `NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has asked your opinion lately, or is about to: about a job, a purchase, a relationship. Ask yourself honestly whether you'd gain anything from what you tell them, or are tempted to leave something out. Kedoshim. The portion that forbids a stumbling block before the blind, which the rabbis read as never misleading anyone who can't see what you see.
Your line: no stumbling blocks. Only you can see behind your own advice. Day four hundred twelve, done.

413.title: Kedoshim: don't stand idly by (Leviticus 19:16)
413.hook: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbor"
413.howItsDone: Jewish law treats rescuing someone in danger as a positive duty, drawn from Leviticus 19:16, and the verse is often cited in Jewish teaching about speaking up for people in danger or being harmed.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, no stumbling block before the blind. Your line was no stumbling blocks. Today, a verse that won't let anyone just watch, and the end of a week.

A person falls on a busy train platform. Plenty of people see it, and each one waits, half-sure somebody else will step forward. Someone is being piled on in a group chat, and the messages get read, one by one, and nobody types a thing. Psychologists call this kind of waiting the bystander effect. Leviticus 19 put the problem into a single verse, long before anyone gave it a name.
screen: `A FALL ON A BUSY PLATFORM.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR SOMEONE.` → `ONE VERSE, LONG BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." Notice the pairing: don't spread stories, and don't stay out of it. Talk too much, or do too little: both fail a neighbor. Literally, the Hebrew says: do not stand upon your neighbor's blood. Standing still while someone bleeds. The translators added idly, and it fits. The Talmud asks where we learn that if you see someone drowning, or dragged off by a wild animal, or attacked by robbers, you are obligated to save them. The answer: from this verse. And it goes further: if you can't save them yourself, you must hire others to help. Maimonides rules that anyone who could save a life and doesn't has broken this commandment. Being present and doing nothing is not neutral. Look back at the week. Azazel carried the wrongs away. Ask the person first. Live by them. Then Kedoshim: holiness for everyone, the corners of the field, no stumbling block, and now this. The Kedoshim days each hand an ordinary person a job. Not the priest. You, on the platform, in the group chat, at the scene.
screen: `NO TALEBEARING, NO STANDING BY.` · `DON'T STAND UPON HIS BLOOD.` · `DROWNING, BEASTS, ROBBERS.` · `A WEEK OF ORDINARY JOBS.` · then, large: `DON'T STAND IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you've been a bystander lately: a coworker everyone talks over, a neighbor who seems to be struggling, a thread where someone's getting piled on. Picture yourself being the one who does something. Not heroic: a question, a call, a message, a word in a meeting.
Kedoshim. The portion that says you may not stand idly by your neighbor's blood: if you can help, you must.
Your line: don't stand idly by. Watching is never quite neutral. Another week of Leviticus, done.
